newsitem.title: USA: Soybean prices fall on US-China trade dispute fears.
newsitem.headline: Soybean prices fall on US-China trade dispute fears.

text.p: Soybean futures on the Chicago Board of Trade fell Monday amid fears that a trade dispute with key importer China could escalate.
In New York, oil prices dropped in New York after a rally Friday as a cold spell continued to grip the U.S. Northeast.

China said Sunday it would suspend temporarily its imports of some U.S. textiles, farm goods, animal husbandry products, fruits and alcoholic drinks in retaliation for Washington's imposition of punitive charges on U.S. purchases of Chinese textiles.
The temporary import ban would take effect Dec. 10.
"There were fears hanging over the market on China's retaliation, but the perceptions are nothing will come of it," said Mark Cermak of O'Connor and Co.
November soybean futures closed 7-3/4 cents a bushel lower at $6.80.
The Knight Ridder Commodity Research Bureau index of 17 futures, however, rose 0.92 points to 240.64, aided by stronger copper prices on New York's Commodity Exchange (COMEX).

Copper rose on expecations that Tuesday's key London Metal Exchange stock data will show a further fall in inventories, which currently stand at a six-year low of 113,400 metric tons. Most expected a drop of about 5,000 tons Tuesday.
Some, however, said the recent slide in copper inventories may be about to come to an end.
December copper closed 1.25 cents up at 95.60 cents a pound.
Cotton futures on the New York Cotton Exchange fell with the U.S. Department of Agriculture poised to increase its U.S. production estimate when it revises its figures Tuesday.
Industry sources estimate U.S. production between 18.4 million and 18.58 million 480-pound bales, compared with USDA's October forecast of 18.159 million.
"The numbers are telling us that there is too much supply chasing too little demand," said David Brandon Jr, a senior economist with Smith Barney.
December cotton settled 0.59 cent weaker at 70.72 cents per pound.

Oil prices ended lower in New York Monday on profit-taking after Friday's rally, which absorbed the price rises from the Northeast's taste of wintry weather, traders said. "I think we were in an overbought situation after Friday," said James Cordier, energy trader at Allendale Inc. in Florida.
The Northeast is the largest heating oil market in the world. Heating oil for December delivery closed off 0.58 cent a
gallon at 68.35 cents on the New York Mercantile Exchange. December crude followed heating oil down, ending 22 cents off at $23.37.
December gasoline settled off 0.25 cent a gallon at 65.02 cents, recovering from lower levels on strength in cash market in the Gulf of Mexico.
Smith Barney meteorologist Jon Davis forecast temperatures 11 to 15 degrees below normal through Friday in the Northeast, causing above-average heating oil demand by consumers.
But, Davis said the cold spell should end by the weekend with temperatures nearly to slightly above normal expected by next week.
